Campus Comparison: Philippians 3:12-16 ("To Live is Christ")

Across all three Calvary Bible Church campuses on November 1, 2026, the pastors preached on Philippians 3:12–16, addressing Paul’s call to press on toward maturity in Christ. While each speaker tailored the message to their unique congregation, the sermons share a unified central message: spiritual effort is a grateful response to Christ's prior pursuit, not an attempt to earn salvation.

---

Shared Themes & Core Message
1. Grace-Driven Effort vs. Earning

All three pastors emphasized the phrase *"because Christ Jesus has made me his own"* (Phil 3:12) to establish that divine grace precedes human exertion. Growth in the Christian life is not about moralistic self-improvement, but responding to a relationship initiated by God.

2. The "Already / Not Yet" Tension of Maturity

Each message highlighted Paul’s admission that despite his spiritual background, he had not yet achieved perfection or final completion. True spiritual maturity is defined not by flawless performance, but by recognizing one's ongoing need for growth while pursuing Christ.

3. Communion Integration

Every campus connected Paul's teaching to the sacrament of Communion. The elements were presented as a visible reminder of Christ’s initial work on the cross and the promise that He will bring His work in believers to completion.

---

Campus-Specific Focus & Application
Boulder Campus (Perry Marshall)

• Theme & Focus: Perry Marshall framed the passage around the "mindset of maturity," defining it through two main qualities: humility (acknowledging room for growth) and confidence (trusting God's initiating and completing work).

• Illustrations & Community Context: Marshall celebrated the Boulder congregation's seasoned believers, highlighting the "Nudge Brothers"—a weekly gathering of men in their 70s and 80s in Niwot who encourage one another in faith. He illustrated relational growth through marriage (comparing a 5-year marriage to 50 years) and academic humility through PhD studies, where deeper learning reveals how much remains unknown.

• Application: Believers are urged to stay consistently committed to life groups, prayer, and community, learning alongside veteran Christians.

Erie Campus (Thomas Milburn)

• Theme & Focus: Thomas Milburn framed the text as a contrast between relational pursuit of Jesus and moralistic religion ("trying to be a good person"). He expanded on Paul's conversion story in Acts 9 to show how God redeems human zeal.

• Theological & Historical References: Preaching on the day after Reformation Day (October 31), Milburn discussed Martin Luther, contrasting infused righteousness with imputed (alien) righteousness. He noted that the Greek word translated "press on" in verse 12 is the same root (*diōkō*) Paul used in verse 6 for "persecute," illustrating how Christ redirected Paul's zeal.

• Illustrations & Application: Quoting Dallas Willard (*"grace is not opposed to effort, but it is opposed to earning"*), Milburn used a sailboat analogy: human effort is raising the sails so the Holy Spirit's wind can push the vessel forward. He challenged listeners to examine their spiritual "diet" (God's Word), prayer, community running partners, and spiritual coaches.

Thornton Campus (Zack Thompson)

• Theme & Focus: Zack Thompson centered his sermon on the theme of living out a newly declared identity. He emphasized that because Christ has declared believers His own, failing to pursue Him is as illogical as accepting a dream job or getting married and remaining on the couch.

• Illustrations & Practical Examination: Thompson opened with three scenarios: getting hired but staying in bed, getting accepted to college but staying home, and getting married but living apart. He defined the "prize" of the upward call as the conclusive experience of knowing Christ fully at the resurrection. To evaluate personal pursuit, he challenged the church to audit their calendars, noting that schedule allocation reveals what prize one is chasing.

• Personal Context & Tone: Thompson shared a conversation with a non-churchgoing friend who assumed "doing my best to be good" was enough, explaining why self-reliance fails before a holy God.

---

Theology / Interpretation Differences

No contradictory theological differences were detected across the three messages. All three pastors presented an identical Reformed understanding of grace, justification by faith alone, and sanctification. 

Minor interpretive variations were strictly homiletical emphasis:

• Erie (Thomas Milburn) explicitly drew upon Reformation terminology (imputed vs. infused righteousness) and highlighted the linguistic link between *diōkō* ("press on" / "persecute") in Philippians 3:6 and 3:12.

• Boulder (Perry Marshall) framed the passage around the subjective "mindset of maturity" (humility paired with confidence in God's Phil 1:6 promise).

• Thornton (Zack Thompson) framed the text around identity and practical alignment, examining how a believer's calendar reflects their pursuit of the prize.

---

Material Differences in What Was Said

Material differences consisted of campus-specific illustrations, personal anecdotes, and local community references:

• Boulder: Cited the "Nudge Brothers" (a Niwot men's group) and "Nudge Sisters," referencing elderly veterans of the faith present at the Boulder campus.

• Erie: Referenced a conversation on an Erie golf course regarding moralism, cited Martin Luther and Reformation Day, quoted Dallas Willard, and referenced Paul Peterson's boat illustration from a prior Boulder message.

• Thornton: Included scripture reading by team member Cheryl Stoddard, utilized the hired/admitted/married introductory illustrations, detailed a personal dialogue with a friend about moral effort, and gave specific operational instructions for four communion stations (front and lobby).
